module_title: Why Sorghum and Millet Are Smart Business in Africa

lessons.title: Comparing sorghum and millet to maize: climate resilience and market demand
lessons.body:
Maize is the most common staple crop in Africa, but it is risky in dry areas. Maize needs 500-800 mm of rain and fails if there is a dry spell during flowering. Sorghum and millet are different. They can survive on 300-500 mm of rain and tolerate temperatures above 35Â°C. In the Sahel, farmers who plant maize often lose everything when rains fail, while sorghum and millet still give 50-70% of a normal harvest. That difference is money in your pocket.

Market demand is also shifting. Breweries like Nigerian Breweries, Guinness Ghana, and SABMiller (now AB InBev) use sorghum and millet to make beer because they are cheaper than imported barley. Flour mills mix sorghum and millet flour with wheat for biscuits, baby food, and porridge. Open-air markets sell these grains daily for food. In 2023, a tonne of sorghum sold for about $250 in Nigeria, while maize sold for $200âbut sorghum often costs less to grow. Millet, though lower in yield, fetches higher prices ($300â$350 per tonne) because it is used in health foods and traditional drinks like kunu.

Climate resilience means you harvest even in bad years. Market demand means you have buyers. Together, they make sorghum and millet a smart business choice. You spend less on irrigation and pesticides, and you can sell to breweries, mills, and local traders. Start by checking which crops your local market wants. Talk to a nearby brewery or flour mill to see if they buy sorghum or millet. Then plan your season around that demand.

lessons.title: Identifying local buyers: breweries, flour mills, and open-air markets
lessons.body:
Before you plant, find your buyer. In most African countries, three main buyers exist: breweries, flour mills, and open-air markets. Breweries are the biggest. In Nigeria, Nigerian Breweries buys over 100,000 tonnes of sorghum each year for its malt drinks and beer. In Ghana, Guinness Ghana uses sorghum and millet. In Kenya, East African Breweries uses sorghum for low-cost beer. These companies often contract farmers in groups and provide seeds and training. To sell to them, you need to meet quality standards: clean grain, less than 14% moisture, and no stones. They also prefer large volumesâat least 5 tonnes.

Flour mills are another buyer. Companies like Honeywell Flour Mills in Nigeria and Pembe Flour Mills in Tanzania buy sorghum and millet to blend with wheat flour. They want white, bold grains with low tannin. You can sell as little as 1 tonne, but you must dry your grain properly. Open-air markets are the easiest entry point. Traders buy in 100 kg bags. In Burkina Faso, a bag of millet sells for $40â$50. In Uganda, sorghum sells for $30â$40 per bag. You can sell directly to market women or through a cooperative.

To find buyers, visit your local market and ask traders what they need. Call the procurement office of a nearby brewery or flour mill. Join a farmer cooperativeâthey often have existing contracts. Start small: plant 1 hectare, sell to the open market, then scale up to a brewery contract. Always agree on price and quantity before harvest to avoid losses.

lessons.title: Calculating potential profit per hectare for sorghum vs. millet
lessons.body:
Letâs do the math for 1 hectare in a savannah zone. For sorghum: you need 10 kg of seed ($10), 50 kg of NPK fertilizer ($30), and labour for land prep, planting, weeding, and harvest ($120). Total cost: $160. A good sorghum yield is 1.5 tonnes per hectare. At $250 per tonne, revenue is $375. Profit = $375 - $160 = $215. For millet: seed costs $8, fertilizer $20, labour $100. Total cost: $128. Yield is lowerâ1 tonne per hectare. At $300 per tonne, revenue is $300. Profit = $300 - $128 = $172. So sorghum gives higher profit per hectare in this example, but millet costs less to grow and is more drought-tolerant.

In drier areas, sorghum yield may drop to 1 tonne, giving profit of $90, while millet stays at 0.8 tonnes, giving profit of $112. So millet wins in very dry zones. Also, if you sell to a brewery, you may get a premium: $280 per tonne for sorghum, raising profit to $260. If you process millet into flour, you can earn $500 per tonne, but you need equipment. For a beginner, start with sorghum if you have moderate rain (400-600 mm) and access to a brewery. Choose millet if you are in the Sahel (300-400 mm) and sell to local markets. Always keep records of your costs and yields to know your true profit.

lessons.title: Understanding drought-tolerant crop advantages in Sahel and savannah zones
lessons.body:
The Sahel is a belt of dry land south of the Sahara, stretching from Senegal to Sudan. Rainfall is 200-600 mm per year, often in one short season. Savannah zones have 600-1000 mm but with dry spells. In both, drought kills maize. Sorghum and millet have special features. Their roots go deepâup to 2 metresâto find water. Their leaves have a waxy coating that reduces water loss. They can stop growing during drought and resume when rain returns. This is called drought escape.

In the Sahel, millet is the most reliable crop. Varieties like SOSAT-C88 and ICMV IS 89305 mature in 75-90 days, escaping late-season drought. Sorghum varieties like Sariaso 14 and CSM 63E mature in 90-110 days and tolerate heat. In savannah zones, you can grow both, but sorghum yields more if rain is good. The advantage is not just survivalâit is stable income. A farmer in Niger with millet harvests at least 500 kg per hectare even in a bad year, while maize gives zero. That 500 kg can feed a family and sell for $150.

Drought tolerance also means less irrigation. You save money on pumps and fuel. You also reduce risk of crop failure, so you can plan your finances. In 2022, a drought hit the Sahel, and maize farmers lost 80% of their crop, but sorghum and millet farmers lost only 20-30%. That is why development agencies like ICRISAT and AGRA promote these crops. For your business, choose drought-tolerant varieties from your national research institute. Plant early with the first rains. Use zaÃ¯ pits or half-moons to catch water. These simple methods can double your yield in dry zones.

lessons.title: Case study: How a smallholder in Nigeria doubled income with millet
lessons.body:
Aisha is a smallholder in Katsina State, northern Nigeria. She used to grow maize on 2 hectares. In 2020, drought hit, and she harvested only 200 kg of maizeâbarely enough to feed her family. She had no money for school fees. In 2021, an extension officer from the Sasakawa Africa Association introduced her to millet. He gave her 5 kg of improved millet seed (variety SOSAT-C88) and taught her to plant in rows with 75 cm spacing, apply 20 kg of NPK per hectare, and use zaÃ¯ pits to capture water.

Aisha planted 1 hectare of millet and 1 hectare of maize. She spent $50 on millet (seed, fertilizer, labour) and $80 on maize. The rains were poor again. Her maize yielded 300 kg, which she sold for $90âa loss. Her millet yielded 1.2 tonnes. She sold 800 kg to a local trader for $240 and kept 400 kg for food. Her profit from millet was $240 - $50 = $190. From maize, she lost $10. Total income from millet was more than double her previous yearâs total income.

In 2022, she planted 2 hectares of millet and no maize. She joined a cooperative that sold to a flour mill in Kano. The mill paid $320 per tonne. She harvested 2.5 tonnes and earned $800. After costs of $120, her profit was $680. She bought a goat and paid school fees. Her advice: âMillet is not a poor manâs crop. It is a business. Use improved seed, plant on time, and find a buyer before you harvest.â Aisha now trains other women in her village.

lessons.title: Setting your first season production goal and budget
lessons.body:
Your first season should be small and focused. Aim to plant 0.5 to 1 hectare of sorghum or millet. A realistic goal is to harvest 1 tonne of sorghum or 0.8 tonnes of millet. That gives you $250â$300 in revenue if you sell to a local market, or more if you get a brewery contract. Write this goal down: âI will plant 1 hectare of sorghum and harvest 1.5 tonnes by [date].â

Now make a budget. For 1 hectare of sorghum in a savannah zone: seed (10 kg improved variety) = $10; fertilizer (50 kg NPK) = $30; labour (land prep, planting, weeding, bird scaring, harvest) = $120; transport to market = $20; total = $180. For millet: seed (5 kg) = $8; fertilizer (25 kg) = $15; labour = $100; transport = $15; total = $138. If you cannot afford fertilizer, use compost or manure. You can also reduce labour by using family labour or a cooperative work group.

To fund your budget, save from other income or take a small loan from a village savings group. Many NGOs and government programmes give free or subsidised seed. Check with your local agricultural extension office. Keep a record book: write down every cost and every sale. After harvest, compare your actual profit to your goal. If you made a profit, increase to 2 hectares next season. If you lost money, find out whyâmaybe poor seed, late planting, or low price. Adjust and try again. Farming is a business; treat it like one.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sorghum & Millet as a Business in Africa

This Practical Reference lesson is your working tool. It pulls together the numbers, buyers, and decision rules you need to treat sorghum and millet as a business â not just a subsistence crop. Keep it open when you plan your season, negotiate with a buyer, or sit down with a lender. Everything here is drawn from official and peer-reviewed sources, with Africa-specific context and a business-first lens.

1. Why sorghum and millet beat maize in the market

Maize is the dominant staple in much of Africa, but it is also the most climate-fragile of the three cereals. Sorghum and pearl millet are C4 cereals with deeper root systems, waxy leaf cuticles, and the ability to suspend growth under stress and resume after rain â traits that make them far more reliable in the Sahel and savannah zones. That reliability translates directly into business value: lower yield variance means more predictable revenue and easier access to credit.

On the demand side, sorghum and millet are no longer "poor people's food." Breweries (notably in Nigeria, Kenya, and Zimbabwe) use sorghum and millet as adjuncts in clear beer and traditional beverages. Flour mills blend them into composite flours for porridge, biscuits, and baby food. Open-air markets and urban supermarkets sell them as wholegrain health foods. This diversified demand base â industrial, institutional, and retail â reduces your price risk compared with maize, which is heavily influenced by government policy and import competition.

2. Identifying local buyers â and what they pay for

Your buyer determines your variety, your quality standard, and your price. In most African markets, four buyer types dominate:

  • Breweries (e.g., Nigerian Breweries, Guinness Nigeria, Delta Beverages in Zimbabwe): buy white sorghum and pearl millet in bulk, typically 20â100 tonnes per contract, with strict moisture (<12%) and aflatoxin specs. Prices are often set in advance, giving you price certainty.
  • Flour mills and food processors: buy sorghum and millet for composite flours, porridge, and snack products. They value consistent grain size, low foreign matter, and traceability.
  • Open-air and urban markets: buy smaller volumes, pay cash, and accept a wider quality range. Margins are lower but entry is easy.
  • Institutions (schools, hospitals, WFP/relief programs): buy in bulk, often through tenders. Requirements are documented and payment is reliable but slower.

Before you plant, visit at least two buyers and ask: What variety? What moisture? What aflatoxin limit? What price per tonne? What delivery point? Write the answers down. This is your production contract in draft form.

3. Profit per hectare: sorghum vs millet vs maize

The table below uses typical smallholder yields and farm-gate prices in West Africa (FAO/ICRISAT ranges). Actual figures vary by country, season, and variety â use them as planning benchmarks, not guarantees.

Table 1. Indicative gross margin per hectare, rain-fed smallholder systems (West Africa, 2023)
Crop Yield (t/ha) Farm-gate price (USD/t) Gross revenue (USD/ha) Variable costs (USD/ha) Gross margin (USD/ha)
Maize (improved, rain-fed)2.0200400180220
Sorghum (improved)1.5260390120270
Pearl millet (improved)1.2300360100260

Source: FAO (2023), FAOSTAT Producer Prices; ICRISAT (2022), Sorghum and Millet Value Chain Analysis â West Africa. Costs include seed, fertilizer, labour, and transport. Sorghum and millet have lower input costs and higher prices per tonne, so their gross margins can exceed maize even at lower yields.

The key business insight: sorghum and millet win on margin, not on volume. They need less fertilizer, less water, and less pesticide than maize, and they sell at a premium to breweries and mills. In a drought year, maize yields can collapse by 50â70%, while sorghum and millet may only drop 20â30%. That stability is worth real money when you have a loan to repay.

4. Drought-tolerant advantages in the Sahel and savannah

The Sahel receives 300â600 mm of rainfall, often in a single erratic season. The savannah zones of Nigeria, Ghana, Burkina Faso, and Sudan have 600â1,000 mm but with dry spells. In both zones, sorghum and millet outperform maize because:

  • They germinate and establish with less soil moisture.
  • They flower earlier and can escape terminal drought.
  • Their deep roots access sub-soil moisture that maize cannot reach.
  • They tolerate high temperatures (35â40Â°C) during grain filling.

For a business, this means you can plant in marginal fields that would fail with maize, and you can plant later if the rains are delayed â a critical flexibility when you are juggling labour and cash flow.

5. Case study: How a smallholder in Nigeria doubled income with millet

Aisha, a 2-hectare farmer in Katsina State, Nigeria, grew maize for years. In 2021, a late-onset rainy season cut her maize yield to 0.8 t/ha, and she sold at 180 USD/t â a gross margin of about 30 USD/ha after costs. In 2022, she switched 1 hectare to improved pearl millet (variety LCIC-MV1) and kept 1 hectare in maize. She sold 1.3 t of millet to a local flour mill at 310 USD/t, and 1.5 t of maize at 200 USD/t. Her millet hectare returned a gross margin of about 300 USD, versus 120 USD for maize. She used the extra cash to buy a second-hand thresher, which cut her post-harvest labour by 40%. By 2023, she had doubled her total farm income and signed a forward contract with the mill for 3 tonnes.

Lesson: The switch was not about yield â it was about price, cost, and reliability. Aisha did not need more land; she needed a better crop-buyer match.

6. Setting your first season production goal and budget

Use this simple budget framework for 1 hectare. Fill in your own local prices.

Table 2. First-season budget template â 1 hectare sorghum or millet (USD)
ItemSorghumPearl milletNotes
Improved seed1512Certified, drought-tolerant variety
Fertilizer (NPK + urea)6045Lower rates than maize
Land preparation & labour5050Ploughing, planting, weeding
Harvest & threshing4040Can be reduced with a thresher
Transport & bags2020To buyer or market
Total variable cost185167Excludes family labour
Expected yield (t/ha)1.51.2Conservative rain-fed
Expected price (USD/t)260300Brewery/mill contract
Expected gross margin205193Before family labour

Source: Adapted from ICRISAT (2022), Sorghum and Millet Value Chain Analysis â West Africa, and FAO (2023), FAOSTAT Producer Prices. Prices vary by country and season; always confirm with a local buyer before planting.

â  SAFETY WARNING â AFLATOXIN AND GRAIN STORAGE

Sorghum and millet can accumulate aflatoxins â toxic compounds produced by moulds â if grain is not dried to below 12â13% moisture and stored in a dry, ventilated place. Aflatoxin-contaminated grain is rejected by breweries and mills and is a serious health hazard. Never sell or consume mouldy, musty, or discoloured grain. Dry on a clean tarpaulin (not on bare ground), test moisture with a cheap meter before storage, and use hermetic bags or clean, dry drums. If you suspect contamination, contact your extension officer or the national food safety authority â do not mix it with clean grain.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Choose your buyer first. Identify at least two local buyers (brewery, mill, market) and confirm variety, moisture, aflatoxin limit, price, and delivery point before planting.
  2. Pick the right crop for your zone. Pearl millet for the driest Sahel fields; sorghum for savannah zones with 400â600 mm; keep maize only on your best-watered land.
  3. Use certified, drought-tolerant seed. Improved varieties (e.g., LCIC-MV1, SAMSORG, CSM series) give 30â50% higher yields than local landraces under stress.
  4. Budget before you plant. Use Table 2 as a template; know your break-even yield and price.
  5. Dry and store properly. Target <12% moisture; use hermetic bags; never store on bare ground.
  6. Keep simple records. Track seed, fertilizer, labour, yield, and sale price per hectare â this is what lenders and contract buyers want to see.
  7. Start small and scale. Plant 0.5â1 ha in your first season, prove the margin, then expand with a forward contract.
  8. Join a farmer group or cooperative. Group sales meet brewery and mill volume thresholds and improve your bargaining power.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Sorghum and Millets (free): global production, nutrition, and market data.
  • ICRISAT â International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (free): drought-tolerant varieties, value chain reports, and agronomy guides.
  • FAOSTAT (free): producer prices, yields, and trade data by country.
  • Africa RISING (IITA/ILRI) (free): smallholder sorghum and millet intensification research in West and East Africa.
  • IITA â International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (free): seed systems, post-harvest handling, and aflatoxin management.

Prepared for Rise AFRICA Skills â Course: Sorghum & Millet Farming. Figures are indicative planning benchmarks; always verify local prices and buyer specifications before committing capital.

quiz.q: What is the minimum rainfall requirement for maize compared to sorghum and millet?
options: A) Maize needs 300-500 mm; sorghum and millet need 500-800 mm
B) Maize needs 500-800 mm; sorghum and millet need 300-500 mm
C) Maize needs 200-300 mm; sorghum and millet need 400-600 mm
D) Maize needs 800-1000 mm; sorghum and millet need 600-800 mm
quiz.explanation: Maize requires more water (500-800 mm) than sorghum and millet, which can survive on 300-500 mm.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a major buyer of sorghum for brewing in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: Nigerian Breweries buys over 100,000 tonnes of sorghum annually for beer production.

quiz.q: What quality standard do breweries typically require for sorghum grain?
options: B) Moisture content below 14% and no stones
quiz.explanation: Breweries need clean grain with less than 14% moisture to prevent spoilage during storage.

quiz.q: In the profit calculation example, what is the profit per hectare for sorghum with a yield of 1.5 tonnes and price of $250 per tonne?
quiz.explanation: Revenue $375 minus total cost $160 equals $215 profit.

quiz.q: Which crop is more profitable in very dry zones (300-400 mm rainfall) according to the lesson?
quiz.explanation: Millet gives higher profit than sorghum in very dry zones because it is more drought-tolerant and costs less to grow.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of sorghum and millet roots in drought conditions?
options: A) They grow shallow to avoid dry soil
B) They grow deepâup to 2 metresâto find water
C) They store water in leaves
quiz.explanation: Deep roots allow sorghum and millet to access water deep in the soil during drought.

quiz.q: Which variety of millet is mentioned as drought-tolerant and early-maturing?
quiz.explanation: SOSAT-C88 is an improved millet variety that matures in 75-90 days, escaping late-season drought.

quiz.q: In the case study, what was Aishaâs profit from millet in 2021?
quiz.explanation: She sold 800 kg for $240 and spent $50, so profit was $190.

quiz.q: What did Aisha do differently in 2022 that increased her income?
options: A) She planted maize instead of millet
B) She joined a cooperative and sold to a flour mill
quiz.explanation: She joined a cooperative that sold to a flour mill, getting a higher price of $320 per tonne.

quiz.q: What is a recommended first-season production goal for a beginner?
options: B) Plant 0.5 to 1 hectare of sorghum or millet
quiz.explanation: Starting small with 0.5 to 1 hectare reduces risk and allows you to learn before scaling up.

quiz.q: What is the total budget for 1 hectare of sorghum in the example?
quiz.explanation: Seed $10 + fertilizer $30 + labour $120 + transport $20 = $180.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended way to reduce costs in your first season?
options: C) Use compost or manure instead of fertilizer
D) Join a cooperative work group
quiz.explanation: Expensive hybrid seed increases costs; improved open-pollinated varieties are cheaper and effective.

quiz.q: What is the main reason breweries prefer sorghum over imported barley?
options: B) Sorghum has higher alcohol content
C) Sorghum is easier to import
quiz.explanation: Sorghum is cheaper than imported barley, reducing production costs for breweries.

quiz.q: In which zone is millet considered the most reliable crop?
quiz.explanation: Millet is most reliable in the Sahel because it is highly drought-tolerant and matures early.

quiz.q: What simple water-harvesting method is mentioned for dry zones?
quiz.explanation: ZaÃ¯ pits are small planting pits that capture and hold rainwater, improving yields in dry areas.

quiz.q: What percentage of a normal harvest can sorghum and millet give when rains fail, compared to maize?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum and millet can still produce 50-70% of a normal harvest in poor rains, while maize often fails completely.

quiz.q: Which organisation is mentioned as promoting sorghum and millet in Africa?
quiz.explanation: ICRISAT (International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics) promotes drought-tolerant crops like sorghum and millet.

quiz.q: What is the price per tonne of millet mentioned in the market demand lesson?
quiz.explanation: Millet fetches higher prices ($300-$350 per tonne) due to demand for health foods and traditional drinks.

quiz.q: What should you do before planting to ensure a market for your crop?
options: A) Wait until harvest to find buyers
B) Talk to local traders, breweries, or flour mills
quiz.explanation: Identifying buyers before planting reduces the risk of post-harvest losses and low prices.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of sorghum over millet in terms of yield?
options: A) Sorghum yields more per hectare
D) Sorghum has higher market price
quiz.explanation: Sorghum typically yields higher (1.5 tonnes/ha) than millet (1 tonne/ha) in moderate rainfall areas.

quiz.q: What record-keeping advice is given for your first season?
options: B) Write down every cost and sale
quiz.explanation: Keeping a record book helps you calculate actual profit and make better decisions next season.

quiz.q: What is a potential premium price for sorghum if sold to a brewery?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that a brewery may pay a premium of $280 per tonne for sorghum.

quiz.q: Which of these is a characteristic of drought-tolerant crops like sorghum and millet?
options: A) Waxy leaves that reduce water loss
quiz.explanation: Waxy leaves help reduce water loss through transpiration, aiding survival in dry conditions.

quiz.q: What did Aishaâs extension officer give her to help start millet farming?
options: A) 5 kg of improved millet seed
quiz.explanation: The extension officer gave her 5 kg of improved millet seed (SOSAT-C88) and training.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for planting millet in rows?
quiz.explanation: The lesson mentions planting in rows with 75 cm spacing for good plant development.

quiz.q: Which of these is a flour mill mentioned in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: Honeywell Flour Mills in Nigeria is mentioned as a buyer of sorghum and millet for blending.

quiz.q: What is the profit per hectare for millet in the example with 1 tonne yield and $300 per tonne price?
quiz.explanation: Revenue $300 minus total cost $128 equals $172 profit.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of drought tolerance for a farmerâs business?
options: A) Less need for irrigation and lower risk of crop failure
quiz.explanation: Drought tolerance reduces irrigation costs and stabilises income by avoiding total crop failure.

quiz.q: What should you do if you make a loss in your first season?
options: B) Find out why and adjust next season
quiz.explanation: Analysing the cause of loss (e.g., poor seed, late planting) helps you improve and succeed next time.

quiz.q: Which of these is a traditional drink made from millet mentioned in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: Kunu is a traditional Nigerian drink made from millet, increasing its market demand.
